doc.title: Cal Collins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 11, 1997

title: Singers' keys, flat keys and why jazz guitarists do not use capos
summary: Talk about playing in different keys, horn transposition, John Cephas's capo use and rock guitarists' tuning and feedback.

people.name: Masters of the Steel String Guitar

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Does it get difficult, mentioning singers, that they’ll say “Body and Soul” could we do it in A or something. Do we have to?

Oh, I love that yeah, I love that. I think there are a lot of guitar players, they love to play in those “bright” keys they call them, you know the A and the E and all that kind of stuff. But some of the newer ones, of course that read real well, they’re used to reading the tenor keys and the alto keys and all that. But yeah, I like to play in those different keys.
Why is it that it seems the majority of standards from the 30s and so forth, are written in flat keys? Do you know why that would be?
I don’t know, it has to do I imagine with the horns, you know B flat for trumpet, A flat or E flat for alto, that kind of thing.
Right. So when they transpose it puts them in good keys.
Yeah, exactly.
Maybe piano players tend to go to the flats more too.
So many singers love to sing in five flats, which is just a half step away from C and I always wonder, why in the world don’t you do them in C instead of D flat?
What would your fellow musicians think if you took out a capo and put it on?
They would say, “What’s that?”
I don’t think I’ve ever seen a jazz guitar player with a capo.

No. Some of the blues players use them quite a bit, some of the old — oh one of my favorites, I was on tour with him, I was on tour twice with, what do they call that, “Masters of the Steel String Guitar” — it’s some kind of endowment thing, arts endowment thing.
Right.
And John Cephas — is that his name?
Yes. John Cephas.

And he would do the slide bar and I just loved him and he was something else. And he would use a capo once in a while, so he could take advantage of the open keys and everything. But jazz guitarists, I don’t know of any that ever did.
If I gave you five bucks, would you do that tonight so we could get it on film?
I would not know how to use it. I really wouldn’t know how to use the thing.
Well some of the rock players nowadays, also, they tune their guitars down a half step I think. And I don’t know the reason for that.

Well I think probably they tune it down because it automatically makes the strings looser, of course they get looser, and they love to bend it and then turn it into the amplifier to make that ridiculous, horrible noise for five minutes or so.
So I trust I’m not going to hear any feedback from you tonight on the stage.
No. No wa-wa pedals, and no feedback, none of that kind of thing.
